text: Everything so far in this chapter answers some version of what's happening inside my resources. AWS CloudTrail answers a completely different question: who did what, and when? It's AWS's control-plane audit log, recording every API call against your account from the console, the CLI from Chapter 5, an SDK, or another AWS service acting on your behalf — the same real split the Azure course drew between Azure Monitor and the Activity Log.

CloudTrail is enabled automatically for every AWS account at no extra charge, recording the last 90 days of activity as Event History, visible right in the console with zero setup. Each event captures who made the call, by IAM identity, what API ran, exactly when, the source IP, and whether it succeeded or failed — enough to answer most recent-incident questions without configuring anything.

For longer retention or cross-region visibility, creating a Trail delivers log files continuously to an S3 bucket, and optionally into a CloudWatch Logs group tying straight back into Lesson 23, for as long as a compliance requirement calls for — years, if needed, well past Event History's 90-day, read-only console window.

CloudTrail splits what it records into two categories. Management events are control-plane operations, like launching an instance or changing an IAM policy, and a Trail logs these by default. Data events are the much higher-volume, object-level calls inside a resource, like an S3 GetObject — not logged by default because of that volume, and turned on deliberately only where object-level visibility is actually needed.

An instance goes down unexpectedly and nobody on the team admits to it. Metrics will show it's stopped, but they can never show who stopped it — CloudTrail does, tying a StopInstances call to an identity's ARN, a timestamp, and a source IP, evidence instead of a guess. Next, Chapter 7 turns to the AWS bill itself, starting with reading it in Cost Explorer.
